The exploits of Madeline were inspired by Bemelmans's own experiences as a rambunctious child in Austria, and the character was influenced by his mother, daughter Barbara, and wife Madeleine. The present illustration comes from Madeline's Christmas, written by Bemelmans in 1956 as a special in McCalls Magazine and published as an independent book in 1985. | | The story takes place on a freezing, blizzardy Christmas Eve in Paris, and Ms. Clavel and all the Girls of the Old House are snowed in. After supper, Madeline hears a knock on the door. The caller is Mustapha, a rug merchant who comes bearing twelve rugs to warm the cold floors of the boarding school. Ms. Clavel gives Madeline the money for these much-needed rugs and Mustapha helps her roll them out onto the floors before venturing back into the blizzard. Soon, though, he grows cold outside without the warmth of his rugs, and he is forced to turn back to the Old House and seek shelter. | | Madeline gives Mustapha medicine, a warm bath, and tea. Fortified and grateful, Mustapha reveals himself to be not only a rug merchant but also a magician. With a whispered Abracadabra, the carpets he had brought take flight, carrying the Girls out above the snow-covered roofs of Paris. Each one is brought home to visit her parents for Christmas Eve. Afterward, they are safely delivered back to the Old House, where Ms. Clavel awaits.

provenance: Boris Mirski Gallery, Boston. | The present private Massachusetts collection (acquired from the previous, 1972). | | N.B. | Leonard Baskin was born in New Jersey, the son of a Rabbi, and was a prolific scholar, draughtsman, sculptor, and teacher. He founded the fine arts press Gehenna Press while a student at Yale in 1942, which would go on to become one of the world's most important art presses, featuring authors like Sylvia Plath, James Baldwin, and Anthony Hecht. Baskin's art often addressed broad, uniting themes centering on Judaism, spirituality, mortality, and social justice. The present work is one of a series on Native American figures that Baskin began in the 1960s. One of Baskin's inspirations for this series was the novel Little Big Man written by Thomas Berger in 1964; the title of the present work is likely a reference to this influence.

The Bearden home frequently hosted such figures as Duke Ellington, Countee Cullen, Paul Robeson, and Mary McLeod Bethune, and the influence of this vibrant environment is evident in Bearden's multifaceted career; he spent time as a cartoonist, a songwriter, a muralist, and a writer. Bearden even dabbled in sports, starting on the Boston University football team (1931-32) and pitching on its baseball team while also playing for the semi-professional, all-Black baseball team the Boston Tigers. | | Much of Bearden's life was spent exploring himself and humanity through art. He wrote that with art "I am trying to find out what there is in me that is common to, or touches, other men" (Bearden in Cedric Dover, American Negro Art (Greenwich, CT: New York Graphic Society, 1960), p. 49). This ethos of exploration led his artistic career through a variety of media, styles, and influences. His early paintings of the American South display the influence of Mexican muralists such as Diego Rivera, while the works he produced after serving in World War II and while traveling through Europe and studying at the Sorbonne are more semi-abstract and avant-garde. In the 1950s, Bearden spent time studying Chinese calligraphy and Dutch Old Masters to develop his grasp of composition and form. By the 1960s he began creating his iconic collages and photostat images. Throughout his career, Bearden sought to explore themes of spirituality, political activism, the African American experience, and humanity, themes that are present in all of his images, from complex and expansive murals to intimate, small-scale pictures such as the present work.

provenance: Purchased directly from the artist in the 1980s. | | N.B. | Corita Kent was a nun, educator, designer, and artist born in Fort Dodge, Iowa. She joined the Sisters of the Immaculate Heart of Mary at age 18 and took the name Sister Mary Corita. After graduating from Immaculate Heart College in Los Angeles and earning her master's degree at the University of Southern California in 1951, Kent took a job leading the art department at Immaculate Heart College. Much of Kent's work during this period was serigraphic, a medium in which she was self-taught; this choice of medium was partially an effort to make art more democratic, accessible, and affordable. Kent was an innovative and progressive teacher and was closely involved in many activist movements, including the anti-Vietnam War movement and the Civil and Women's Rights movements. | | In the 1960s Kent moved to Boston, where she began a particularly prolific period of creation. One of Kent's works is likely very familiar to local Bostonians: the iconic 1971 Rainbow Swash mural on the LNG storage tank in Dorchester - the largest copyrighted artwork in the world. A maquette of this work is being sold in the present sale. She also designed the 1985 Love stamp for the USPS. Kent died in Watertown, Massachusetts, in 1986.

His father was a well-known musician and composer with the Stuttgart Philharmonic Orchestra until 1933, when he was forced out by Hitler's regime. At around this time the Kahns fled Germany; Wolf's siblings and parents went to the United States while he was sent to live with his grandmother in Frankfurt. Wolf finally reunited with his family in New York in 1940. Over the following decades, Wolf took art classes in and around New York City, including with New School's Stuart Davis and Abstract Expressionist Hans Hofmann. He completed a bachelor's degree at the University of Chicago in 1950 and eventually settled down with his wife, Emily Mason, in Brattleboro, Vermont. | | Kahn's early work was more monochromatic than his later work. When he moved to Vermont he developed a new focus on the foggy, atmospheric New England landscape and Maine coastline. Kahn's landscapes apply an evocative, vibrant blend of Realism, Impressionism, and Color Field painting. His works demonstrate the influence of the variety of artist with whom he worked throughout his career, including impressionists, modernists, and abstract artists, to create a style wholly unique and identifiable as his. | | Wolf Kahn's work is held in many large collections including the Metropolitan Museum of Art, the Art Institute of Chicago, the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston, the National Gallery of Art, the Whitney Museum of Art, and the Smithsonian American Art Museum.

After his death in Boston in 1916, many of his works were placed into storage in a Back Bay warehouse by his family, where they were soon forgotten. Only in the late 1950s, when that warehouse was scheduled for demolition, were the paintings discovered, and the Vose Galleries in Boston played a crucial role in promoting both Enneking and his oeuvre thereafter. | | Enneking was a plein air painter and was particularly interested in the atmospheric effects of the light in different seasons and at different times of day. provenance: Passed down in the family of the present owner since at least the 1930s. | | N.B. | Edward Hill's family came to Massachusetts from Staffordshire, England, when Edward was only 1 year old. The family moved frequently around the Boston area, and Hill would eventually move to Littleton and then Lancaster, New Hampshire, in the mid-1870s. Hill became the artist-in-residence at the Profile House hotel in Franconia Notch (burned down in 1923) in around 1875, and held this role for 15 years. During this time he traveled around painting nearly every aspect of the iconic White Mountain landscape, including Profile Lake, Echo Lake, The Flume, and Mount Lafayette. Hill's paintings of the surrounding landscape that he produced during this period were popular souvenirs among the hotel's affluent guests. The present painting likely comes from Hill's time at the Profile House; the brooks and ponds around Franconia Notch were popular sites for trout fishing.

Denis Glover (by descent from the artist). | | N.B. | Artist and environmentalist Doris ("Dolly") Lindo Lewis (Henriquez) divided her life among New York, Massachusetts, the Caribbean, and South Florida. Now recognized as a pioneer of surrealism and environmental activism, Lewis is known for her explorations of fertility, creation, and woman's place within the natural world. Lewis was born in 1909 in San Jose, Costa Rica, and later moved to Cambridge, Massachusetts, with her mother. She spent much of her youth summering in Cape Cod became associated with several New York, Boston, and Cape Cod artists and writers including Dodge MacKinght, Howard Gibbs, Harold Dunbar, and Byron Thomas. During this early period, she painted primarily traditional Cape landscapes, which she exhibited in and around Cambridge. In the 1930s Lewis shifted to more surrealistic work which she exhibited at the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston, and the Provincetown Art Association. In 1937, Lewis married Anglo-Jamaican Edward Henriquez in Havana, where she spent the next twelve years. The two later returned to the states, moving to Florida in 1949, where she began to explore modernism, iron sculpture, and pottery. Lewis played a courageous role in Florida's environmental affairs and was credited by Marjory Stoneman Douglas, known for her staunch defense of the Everglades, as a leading force in environmental activism. Doris Lindo Lewis died in 1995 at her home in West Palm Beach. Her works are held in the permanent collections of the Boston Museum of Fine Arts, the Los Angeles County Museum of Art, Washington's National Gallery, and the Provincetown Art Association and Museum, among others.

description: Still Life with Fruit and a Jug signed 'BENEKER' (lower right); signed 'Beneker' and with an oil portrait of a woman (on the reverse) oil on board 23 3/4 x 20 in. (60.3 x 50.8 cm) framed 31 3/4 x 27 3/4 x 1 1/2 in. (80.6 x 70.5 x 3.8 cm)
provenance: Gail Feingarten Oppenheimer Collection, Beverly Hills. | A private collection (by descent from the previous). | Sale, Bonhams, Los Angeles, The Collection of Gail Feingarten Oppenheimer, March 9, 2022, lot 98. | The present private collection (acquired from the previous). | | N.B. | Beneker was grew up in Michigan, studied at the Chicago Art Institute and New York Arts Student League, and spent many summers in Truro, Massachusetts. He was a founder of the Provincetown Art Association and Museum. During World War I, Beneker was commissioned to illustrate posters for the war effort, and much of his best-known work comes from this period. Much of Beneker's work portrays a sort of romanticized industrialism, an idealization of the common laborer and an ode to the honor of working Americans. This message was a distinctly contemporary one. He even held artist residencies at corporations like General Electric, Rohm & Hass, and Hydraulic Pressed Steel. | | The present work offers a twofold vision of Beneker's output. On the reverse is a portrait of a woman, simple and staid in conservative colors - typical of Beneker's portraiture. On the front, a still life reflects the same geometric forms and industrial palette. There is even a certain sparseness to the spread on the table; as far as still lifes go, it is overtly and intentionally bare, with four apples, a bunch of grapes, and an unadorned pewter pitcher.

title: Still Life with Fruit and Bread
description: Still Life with Fruit and Bread signed 'Knaths' (lower left); with labels from Christie's and Eldred's, and a fragmentary Los Angeles Exposition label (affixed to the stretcher and backing) oil on canvas 18 x 18 in. (45.7 x 45.7 cm) framed 23 x 23 x 1 in. (58.4 x 58.4 x 2.5 cm)
provenance: The collection of Mr. and Mrs. Joseph Hoenigsberg. | A private New York collection. | Wright, New York, The Lyrical Line, May 23, 2006, lot 937. | Christie's, New York, Interiors, March 4, 2008, lot 94. | A private Cape Cod, Massachusetts, collection. | Eldred's, Massachusetts, The Summer Sale, July 26, 2024, lot 5724. | The present private collection (acquired from the previous). | | N.B. | Karl Knaths was born in Eau Claire, Wisconsin, and grew up in nearby Portage. After graduating high school, he studied at the Milwaukee Art Institute and then at the School of the Art Institute of Chicago. In 1919, after a stint as a scenery painter and a couple years of military service, Knaths moved to Provincetown, Massachusetts, where he would live for most of his life. Knaths continued painting up until his death in 1971, becoming undoubtedly one of the leading American modernists of his time. From the 1950s onward, Knaths (like all American modernists at the time) experienced the threat of an impending shift toward a new era of abstract expressionism, although the market for his work never entirely waned. | | Knaths's work displays the influence of European modernism, to which he was exposed early on at the 1913 Armory Show in Chicago. The muted colors and blocked shapes of Cézanne were particularly appealing to him, and his mature post-1930 oeuvre reflects the exploration of color and proportion spurred on by his close study of Cubism, European modernism, and of Bauhaus design. In 1952, Knaths told the Philadelphia Inquirer that his style evolved as he "learned to move slowly from color relations, to line sequence, to better spacing, proportions, to a thematic play of shapes." This relates the distinctly theoretical bent to Knaths's artistic practice. | | Knaths's still lifes are fascinating examples of his theoretical and artistic journeys. The present work's rhythmic, lyrical composition, calligraphic lines, and sharply demarcated color blocks shows his application of the theories of European modernism and Bauhaus design while still maintaining the figural clarity of Cézanne. Knaths's modernism was pioneering at its time, and it is not difficult to see how truly pioneering it was in this engaging, carefully planned, and lively work.
